name: Business Numbers & Unit Economics Engine
tag: A reality check for your numbers: customer cost vs. value, break-even, cash runway and what your time is worth.

scenarios.title: Is my ad spend paying off?
scenarios.ask: I spend ${spend} a month on ads and get {customers} new customers. Each orders about ${order} and comes back {repeat} times.
steps: CAC calculator
Cost to get a customer: ${spend} / {customers} = ${=round(spend / customers, 2)}.
LTV calculator
Lifetime gross profit at a 40% margin: {repeat} orders x ${order} x 0.4 = ${=round(repeat * order * 0.4, 2)}.
Comparer
Each customer returns {=round(repeat * order * 0.4 / (spend / customers), 1)} times what they cost to get.
Advisor
A ratio near 3 or more is commonly treated as healthy. Below 1 means each customer loses money.

result.title: Customer economics
rows: Orders to earn back ad cost

followups: Why use gross profit instead of revenue?
Revenue includes what the product costs you. Using gross profit shows what's really left to pay for ads and overhead.
Change the margin in the full app. Here, every 10 points of margin moves lifetime profit by ${=round(repeat * order * 0.1, 2)}.

scenarios.title: When do I break even?
scenarios.ask: My fixed costs are ${fixed} a month. I sell at ${price} and each sale costs me ${cost} to make.
steps: Margin
Each sale leaves ${=max(1, price - cost)} after its direct cost.
Break-even
You need {=ceil(fixed / max(1, price - cost))} sales a month to cover fixed costs.
Daily target
That's about {=ceil(fixed / max(1, price - cost) / 26)} sales per working day.
Sensitivity
A 10% price rise would cut the sales you need to {=ceil(fixed / max(1, price * 1.1 - cost))}.
followups: What if cost is higher than price?
Then every sale loses money and no volume fixes it. The engine treats profit per sale as at least $1 here so the math still shows, but you'd need to reprice.
Maybe. The engine shows how many customers you could lose and still earn the same. Testing a price change on new customers first is lower risk.

scenarios.title: What's my time worth?
scenarios.ask: My business makes ${profit} profit a month and I work {hours} a week. Should I hire help at ${wage} an hour?
steps: Rate calculator
Your effective rate is ${=round(profit / (hours * 4.33), 2)} an hour.
Task sorter
Sorted your tasks. About {=round(hours * 0.3)} hours a week are admin anyone trained could do.
Comparer
Help would cost ${=round(hours * 0.3 * wage * 4.33)} a month for those hours.
Advisor
Hiring pays if you use the freed hours on work that earns more than ${wage} an hour.
followups: What if I just take the time off?
That's a fair choice. The engine shows the cost of the time back, which is ${=round(hours * 0.3 * wage * 4.33)} a month here.
Not in this quick view. The full app lets you add payroll taxes and benefits to the hourly cost.
